html:
The Tobacco Protest was a nationwide revolt in Iran in 1891 and 1892 against a monopoly over the country's tobacco that Naser al-Din Shah of the Qajar dynasty had sold to a British businessman, Major Gerald Talbot, in 1890.

Merchants, who would lose their trade, and the Shia clergy led the protest. In December 1891 a fatwa, credited to the senior cleric Mirza Hasan Shirazi in Iraq, declared smoking forbidden. Iranians stopped smoking across the country; it was said even the shah's wives gave up their water pipes.

In January 1892 the shah cancelled the concession and had to pay a heavy penalty. The protest showed the power of the clergy and the bazaar together, a pattern seen again in the Constitutional Revolution of 1905 and the Iranian Revolution of 1979. See also Iran.
